newsitem.title: USA: U.S. financial reform gets push from Treasury.
newsitem.headline: U.S. financial reform gets push from Treasury.

text.p: The drive to modernize the U.S. financial services industry got a boost Wednesday from proposals put forward by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, but there was also criticism that the administration was ducking some of the bigger controversies.

"I think this starts with a good degree of momentum," said Geoffrey Miller, director of the New York University law school's center for the study of central banks. "I do think that sooner or later the (depression era) Glass-Steagall law is going to be repealed."

In general, participants in different segments of the industry said they were pleased Rubin was taking a position. They also thought the move could help break a logjam that has up to now prevented reform. Rubin's proposal would allow banks to make further moves into securities and insurance than they have been able to accomplish so far.

"We believe that the Treasury proposal is a constructive step twoward what we hope will be quick action in this session of Congress to reform the regulatory structure for financial services in this country," said James Wiggins, a spokeman for Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, the largest U.S. broker.
Wiggins added the current framework is a "one-way street" that permits banks to buy securities firms but bars securities firms from buying all but a small interest in a bank.

"We think there needs to be a level playing field so that companies can compete on the basis of service, innovation and capital strength as opposed to just some regulatory structure that doesn't make sense any more," Wiggins said.

"Given the technology and the way everything is moving these days at a very rapid rate, we're going to have to come up with a level playing field for everybody," said Perrin Long, an independent analyst who tracks the securities industry. He said it was important that Rubin is now out in public moving the process along.

But Charles Gabriel, a political analyst with Pruidential Securities, said Rubin's approach "exacerbates the one-way street we already have." He said it would still be easier for banks to go into insurance and securities businesses rather than the other way around.
Gabriel said he also detected a "backing away" from some fairly strong statements Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke has made recently on mixing banking and non-financial commerce.
In a statement, Frank Newman, chairman and Chief executive of Bankers Trust New York Corp, called the Rubin proposals "welcome and thoughtful news" for advocates of reform and modernization.

"Secretary Rubin's advocacy of measures to promote greater competitiveness, both among U.S. institutions and in their ability to compete with foreign institutions, deserves the strong support of both providers and users of financial services," Newman aid.

Bankers Trust in April agreed to acquire Alex. Brown Inc in a deal that would not have been possible without the decision of the Federal Reserve to expand the amount of underwriting that banks can do in a securities affiliate.

The Securities Industry Association (SIA), trade group for investment banks and brokers, said in a statement it was pleased Treasury was taking a stand but it has some continuing concerns. One of the concerns, the SIA said, was in the area of functional regulation. The SIA has long argued each area of the financial servcies should be subject to the same regulation.
Gary Hughes, vice president and chief counsel for securities and banking at the American Council of Life Insurance, said "our feeling is that he lays out a concept that we find very encouraging."
He said the proposals "seem to us to be headed in the right direction especially with the acknowledgment that there ought to be functional regulation of insurance."
"It's an importanty contribution to the ongoing debate," said Raphael Soifer, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman.

Soifer said the old debate about the depression-era Glass Steagall law separating banking and securities into different areas has become old hat while "the more contentious areas now are insurance and even more so the whole banking and commerce area."

Rubin outlined two scenarios for joining banks and commercial firms. One plan would allow limited combinations but with the 1,000 largest non-financial firms excluded. Another would bar mixing with banks but permit thrift institutions to combine with commercial firms as now allowed.
